title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable
event_hint: arXiv publication on agent harness evolution methodology
problem: Behavior localization is the central bottleneck in harness evolution. Before a modification can be made, developers or coding agents must identify all code locations that implement the target behavior. This is difficult because production harnesses are large, tightly coupled, and behaviorally distributed across files, functions, execution stages, and state transitions, while modification requests describe what the system should do and repositories are organized by files and modules.
mechanism: Harness Handbook: a behavior-centric representation synthesized automatically from a harness codebase through static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring, which organizes implementation knowledge around system behaviors and links each behavior to corresponding source code. Also introduces Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), which guides coding agents from high-level behavior descriptions to relevant implementation details and verifies candidate locations against current source.

evidence.claim: Harness Handbook organizes implementation knowledge by what the harness does rather than by files and modules, using a three-level hierarchy (L1: system overview, L2: component overview, L3: unit deep dive) with progressive disclosure and behavior-implementation alignment rules.

The construction pipeline uses static analysis to extract program facts (call graph, state accesses, external calls), behavioral organization to map functions to execution stages via a propose-review loop, and hierarchical synthesis to build the L1-L3 handbook.
Overall win rates improve by 10.0 percentage points on Codex and 18.9 percentage points on Terminus-2, while planner token use decreases by 12.7% and 8.6% respectively.
evidence.condition: Percentage point improvement in overall win rate (Codex: +10.0, Terminus-2: +18.9); planner token reduction (Codex: -12.7%, Terminus-2: -8.6%)

evidence.claim: Evaluated on Terminus-2 and Codex, two open-source agent harnesses. Terminus-2 uses function-as-leaf mode with a reliable seed skeleton; Codex uses file-as-leaf mode to infer hierarchy at repository scale. Each harness contributes 30 behavior-driven modification requests.
evidence.condition: Open-source agent harnesses (Terminus-2, Codex); 30 modification requests per harness

evidence.claim: Modification requests are grouped into Query (modifies existing behavior without revealing target locations), Cross-file (adds end-to-end capability spanning files/modules), and Search-Hostile (places relevant implementations in locations hard to recover by keyword search). Requests are also labeled Easy, Medium, or Hard by localization difficulty.
evidence.condition: Three request types: Query, Cross-file, Search-Hostile; three difficulty levels: Easy, Medium, Hard

evaluation_context: Evaluated on two open-source agent harnesses (Terminus-2 and Codex) with 30 behavior-driven modification requests per harness. Comparison between Baseline planning (direct repository exploration) and Handbook-Assisted BGPD planning. Plan quality judged independently by three models (GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) scoring on Localization (50% weight), Scope Control (25%), and Reasoning (25%). Localization accuracy measured via Recall, Precision, F1, and Wrong metrics at file and symbol granularity against independent reference plans.
limitations: EXPLICIT: None stated in visible evidence. REMAINING GAPS: Specific baseline values for plan quality scores (numerical scores for Localization, Scope Control, Reasoning dimensions) are not visible in supplement. The supplement provides win rate improvements and token reductions but not the absolute baseline scores. Repository characteristics (code size, number of functions, modules) are not provided. Index construction overhead and refresh cost information remains not visible.
project_relevance: DIRECTLY RELEVANT to Agent semantic acceleration (Agent Acceleration topic, Read/Grep direction). The supplement now provides quantitative evidence: Handbook-Assisted planning achieves 10.0-18.9 percentage point improvements in win rates while reducing planner tokens by 8.6-12.7%. On Terminus-2, F1 scores reach 77.1-89.3% and precision reaches 93.3%. Wrong (complete localization failures) decreases by up to 25.9 points. Gains persist across Query (+26.7), Search-Hostile (+33.3), and Cross-file (+16.3 to +20.0) request types. Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure reduces repeated Read/Grep/tool calls by guiding agents directly to relevant code locations. The approach focuses on behavior-to-code mapping rather than repository indexing acceleration, which is a different angle from traditional code graph/repo graph approaches. Specific evidence on absolute end-to-end task latency reduction remains not visible.

evidence_gaps.question: What are the two open-source agent harnesses used in evaluation and what are their characteristics (code size, number of functions, modules)?
